title: A Five-Dimensional Business Ontology for Proactive Data Services in Upstream Oil and Gas
abstract: Abstract Upstream oil and gas operators have built substantial digital foundations, including unified data standards, enterprise data lakes, domain-specific applications, and knowledge graphs. Even with these foundations in place, engineers performing reservoir assessment, well-performance diagnosis, production optimization, and field-development planning still spend considerable effort searching data catalogs, system menus, database tables, and technical documents to assemble the resources needed for a specific task. Conventional data models describe structure, ingestion, and access, but they do not fully capture the engineering context in which a resource is used, its role in the workflow, the rules governing its use, or the conditions under which it should be delivered. This paper introduces a five-dimensional business ontology that places upstream petroleum work in a semantic coordinate space defined by object, business, work, discipline, and process. Each valid coordinate identifies one Minimum Business Unit (MBU), which acts as the shared anchor for attaching resources, governing knowledge-graph content, and delivering task-relevant data on demand. The architecture separates KG0, the standard business-ontology layer of professional concepts, resource profiles, and rules, from KG1, the enterprise instance-knowledge layer of actual assets, data, documents, tools, cases, and evidence. Heterogeneous resources are represented through a three-layer envelope comprising a common identity and governance layer, a resourceDefinition layer for schemas and semantic relationships, and an instanceStorage layer for payloads, storage bindings, runtime state, validation, and integrity control. The method was implemented in an operational pilot at a large oil and gas operator. At the deployment snapshot, KG0 contained 20,940 valid MBUs; KG1 registered 137,310 unique resources and business-context mappings for 12,022 production wells; and the resource bindings covered approximately 300,000 file versions of reports, experimental records, and geological drawings. More than 160 upstream engineering analysis scenarios were supported in actual use. A retrospective, process-based operational estimate for a representative mature reservoir-performance-analysis workflow indicated that manual data-preparation effort fell from approximately 45–55% of active person-hours (representative value, approximately 50%) to approximately 1.5–2.7% (representative value, approximately 2.2%, and below 3%) after task-relevant resources had been governed, registered, and delivered through the business context. These results indicate that the five-dimensional ontology and MBU anchoring method can provide a scalable and traceable semantic layer between underlying data models and business knowledge graphs. The technical contribution is the ontology and its MBU-based anchoring mechanism; the service platform is the environment in which that mechanism is implemented.

title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game
abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.

evidence.title: Four Bridges: Measuring Deception Propensity in a Multi-Agent Game
evidence.abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed in settings where they interact and coordinate with other agents, yet honesty is mostly measured in single-turn, single-agent benchmarks that pressure the model to deceive. We study deception that emerges in multi-agent interaction without any instruction to deceive. We introduce Kradle, a platform for evaluating AI models, and Four Bridges, an information asymmetry game in which four agents distribute across four rooms: one is the death room, the others hold food worth more if not shared. One agent, the informed agent, knows which room is the death room and can withhold or disclose that information. We evaluate eight frontier models as the informed agent. Deceptive behavior appears in every model and in 73% of all runs (6% to 100% per model), and does not decrease with capability tier within a model family. When the informed agent does disclose, the warning is often challenged, and agents that challenge it enter the death room twice as often as those that do not. Telling all agents that one of them knows the death room collapses deception in six of eight models; telling the informed agent that the room is permanently fatal moves only one. On an open-weight model, an honesty steering vector reduces deception to 0% and adversarial honesty training to 6%. The platform and game provide a testbed for measuring deceptive behavior and comparing interventions.

title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock's 4.46times to 10.87times with one request, and from 1.94times to 3.93times with batching.

title: Active Learning-Assisted Human-In-The-Loop Framework for Rapid Borehole Image Annotation: Enabling AI-Powered Geological Interpretation at Scale
abstract: Abstract Borehole image interpretation is a cornerstone of subsurface characterization in the oil and gas industry, providing high-resolution, azimuthally oriented data for in-situ stress estimation, wellbore stability assessment, and reservoir quality evaluation. Despite its geological significance, this process remains largely manual: expert geologists must individually review and annotate high-resolution image logs that can span thousands of feet per well, investing hundreds of hours per project before any automated prediction is available. This paper presents an integrated Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) active learning framework designed to overcome this annotation bottleneck. The system supports detection of geological features, particularly formation dips, from acoustic and resistivity image logs. It operates through three concurrent modules: (1) an interactive annotation interface overlaying model predictions on borehole images for expert review and correction; (2) an asynchronous background training engine leveraging the DINOv3 visual foundation model for deep feature extraction and continuous refinement of a lightweight convolutional segmentation head; and (3) an active learning selection module employing entropy-based uncertainty sampling that identifies and prioritizes the most informative depth intervals. Experimental results show that uncertainty sampling provides a measurable early-round advantage. Between 20 and 160 annotated images in the reference-well experiment, uncertainty sampling increases mean IoU by 1.74% and mean Dice/F1 by 1.44% relative to sequential depth-order selection. It also reaches a predefined early-convergence criterion of a mean angular error below 10° for two consecutive rounds, with a decrease in the confirming round, using 50 annotated images compared with 60 for sequential selection (16.7% fewer annotations). Validation across four wells, including the reference well, shows that uncertainty sampling reduces the annotation volume required to reach 95% of final IoU by 24.3% on average, with well-specific reductions ranging from 0% to 62.5%. In the architecture comparison, DINOv3 Projected Layers 3&6 outperforms DINOv3 Full Features across all three metrics, achieving 4.84° ± 0.25° angular error, 0.4409 ± 0.0071 IoU, and 0.6084 ± 0.0075 Dice/F1 with approximately 48,000 trainable parameters.

title: Should We Combine Our Data? Algorithms and Limits for Privately Assessing Data Sharing
abstract: In this paper, we study when two parties should pool their data to train a machine learning model. Two agents, Alice and Bob, each hold a sensitive labeled dataset and want to train a classifier from a given hypothesis class $\mathcal{H}$. Even when each party's dataset can be perfectly classified on its own, the two parties may follow conflicting labeling standards or have selection biases that affect their features and label sets, such that no single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ fits their combined data. Before committing to data sharing, Alice and Bob therefore want to test whether a single classifier in $\mathcal{H}$ can jointly fit both datasets---without revealing their individual data points to one another. We formalize this problem from a learning-theoretic viewpoint via $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}$, the minimum \emph{number of mistakes} made by any hypothesis in $\mathcal{H}$ on their pooled data. Through interactive communication, the agents must distinguish $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}=0$ (compatible datasets) from $\operatorname{opt}_\mathcal{H}\geq t$ (conflicting datasets) under pure $\varepsilon$-two-party differential privacy. A trusted curator could do this with $t=O(1/\varepsilon)$, and we ask how small $t$ can be without one. For thresholds on the real line over a domain of size $m$, we show that the optimal $t$ is $\tildeΘ(\log\log m/\varepsilon)$, exponentially smaller than the $Θ(\log m/\varepsilon)$ samples needed to privately learn thresholds, even with a curator. For halfspaces in $\mathbb{R}^d$, the dependence on $m$ jumps to $\log(m)$: we give a protocol with $t=\tilde{O}(d^3\log m/\varepsilon)$ and show that some domains require $t=Ω(d\log(m/d)/\varepsilon)$.

title: RoboColosseum: Evaluating Physical Intelligence at Scale In-The-Wild
abstract: General-purpose robot policies must work across robots, tasks, and environments, yet the variation that makes physical trials informative also makes them difficult to reproduce. We introduce RoboColosseum, a distributed evaluation framework that combines unified policy serving and standardized protocols across a network of locally operated robots in diverse environments. Our initial study evaluates five vision-language-action (VLA) policies and three frontier AI agents across four embodiments (SO-101, Franka, Bimanual-YAM, and G1 Humanoid). The Open Track compares models without task-specific adaptation in blinded, pairwise trials under matched local conditions. The Fine-tune Track measures how well VLA policies adapt to 20 tasks across all four embodiments when each policy receives the same 100 demonstrations per task. Across 5,699 pairwise Open Track comparisons at 124 sites, frontier agents rival specialized VLA policies, while all systems struggle to complete open-world tasks reliably. After fine-tuning, GR00T N1.7 leads on SO-101 and pi0.5 leads on Franka and Bimanual-YAM. Policy rankings show weak agreement across embodiment-specific task suites (Kendall W = 0.24). Open Track rankings poorly predict relative performance after fine-tuning, with substantial rank reversals on all three embodiments shared between tracks. Measuring partial progress reveals differences that task success alone misses. On the G1 Humanoid, no policy completes any of the five tasks, yet average progress ranges from 13.3% to 23.2% across policies. Open Track rankings stabilize as trials accumulate, and active matchmaking achieves comparable ranking agreement with substantially fewer physical trials than uniform sampling. These results show how distributed physical evaluation can reveal where robot policies generalize, how well they adapt to new tasks, and how far they progress on tasks they fail to complete.

title: Scalable GenAI-Driven UNSPSC Classification for Oil & Gas Industry Material Master
abstract: Abstract The United Nations Standard Products and Services Code (UNSPSC) provide a globally recognized hierarchical taxonomy for classifying materials and services, enabling spend visibility, category management, inventory rationalization, supplier consolidation, and regulatory reporting across enterprise procurement functions. However, large oil and gas organizations often maintain material masters containing hundreds of thousands of records accumulated over decades of operations. These records typically consist of short technical descriptions that are heavily abbreviated, domain-specific, and inconsistently maintained, making accurate manual classification against the approximately 150,000-code UNSPSC taxonomy time-consuming, costly, and difficult to sustain as the taxonomy evolves. This paper presents a Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) based classification framework designed specifically for industrial material master data. The solution employs a two-stage architecture. The first stage performs catalog-scale Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) query refinement over the full UNSPSC taxonomy, classifying each material record to a UNSPSC Commodity code. Prior to retrieval, CoT reasoning normalizes descriptions, expands abbreviations, and surfaces technical attributes that improve retrieval quality. To maintain consistency of predictions across the growing corpus of previously classified materials, a second stage incorporates a SME-validated Knowledge Base containing previously confirmed material-to-UNSPSC mappings. When an incoming material closely matches an existing validated record, the Knowledge Base ensures that it receives a classification consistent with prior expert decisions, eliminating prediction drift across similar material types encountered in past classification activities. Every SME-confirmed output is written back into the Knowledge Base, forming a continuous learning loop that requires no model retraining. A systematic ablation study was conducted to quantify the contribution of each architectural component. Experiments evaluated retrieval strategy, embedding model selection, semantic reranking, embedding scope, query refinement, knowledge-base grounding, and large language model choice. Retrieval performance was measured using Recall@K and Mean Reciprocal Rank, while end-to-end performance was evaluated at the UNSPSC Segment, Family, Class, and Commodity levels. Using a stratified SME-labeled benchmark spanning upstream, midstream, and downstream materials, the optimized pipeline achieved 75.0% Commodity-level accuracy compared with approximately 6% for a zero-shot large language model baseline, while operating at approximately 500 times the throughput of manual SME classification. The approach has been successfully applied to hundreds of thousands of material records and provides a scalable, explainable, and taxonomy-adaptive design pattern for large-scale industrial classification problems.

title: Structured Visual Landscape: Generating Preferred Representations in Biological and Artificial Neural Networks
abstract: Understanding how neurons respond to visual stimulus is an important question in both deep learning and neuroscience. It has significant implications for enhancing the interpretability of black-box artificial neural networks and for understanding the visual representation in the human brain. We propose a structured visual representations landscape and design an activation-based prior that allows us to effectively regularize the landscape with activations from brain regions or neural network units. Our model Vis-Lens integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model into an image generation framework. It enables the generation of natural, realistic preferred images by directly modifying the activation-regularized latent codes without per-image iterative optimization. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework on both artificial neural networks and human visual cortex using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Our framework improves activation modulation and image realism compared with a recent state-of-the-art method for generating preferred visual representations of these neural targets.

title: Harvesting SWE Benchmarks from Wild Vibe Coding Sessions
abstract: Development teams need reproducible tasks from their own repositories and workflows to evaluate coding agents. Conversational developer-agent collaboration ("vibe coding") produces abundant coding sessions and repository checkpoints, but requirements evolve across turns, unrelated conversations co-occur with commits, and engineering efforts can span multiple sessions. We present SessionFarmer, an automated framework that turns these records into self-contained, executable software engineering tasks. It analyzes dialogue and commit history to filter unrelated sessions and group multi-turn, potentially multi-session interactions into work episodes centered on one engineering goal. For each episode, it reconstructs a hermetic execution container, synthesizes a task statement from the full context, and authors repository-grounded engineering-quality rubrics and unit tests. Closed-loop test refinement uses requirement-breaking mutants and a blind solver to reduce false rejections of valid alternatives and false acceptances of incomplete solutions. We construct CropChat, an open benchmark of 242 tasks across 61 public repositories and 14 programming languages, and CropEnterprise from proprietary enterprise logs. In a CropEnterprise audit, the original developers endorse the vast majority of reconstructed episode boundaries, task statements, and quality rubrics. Full-episode context covers substantially more user requirements than single-turn or single-session inputs. Test refinement cuts false-rejection rates and raises balanced accuracy against reference patch labels by 7-9 percentage points across solvers. Across 12 model-harness configurations on CropChat, the strongest setup achieves 39.3% Pass@1, while harness choice shifts Pass@1 by up to 8.4 percentage points for the same model.

title: Measurement data and code for "Beyond the Thirty-Second Window: Duration, Not Memory, in a Fixed-Frame TTS Model"
abstract: This record accompanies the preprint "Beyond the Thirty-Second Window: Duration, Not Memory, in a Fixed-Frame TTS Model" (preprint: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23637738). It contains every script and every table that produces a number in the paper, the protocol documents, the de-identified exports of the listening panel, and the exact audio files the panel heard. It contains no model weights and not the full generated-audio set — see "What is not here" in README.md. Contents (569 files, 268.5 MB unpacked): analysis/ (238 files), audio/ (182), benchmark/ (87), data/ (30), docs/ (6), figures/ (6), protocol/ (7), paper/ (5), numbers/ (3), plus LICENSE, LICENSE-DATA, NOTICE, README.md and MANIFEST.csv. MANIFEST.csv lists every file with its size and MD5 checksum. This is the first public release of this dataset, published as version v1 on 2026-11-02 alongside version v2 of the preprint.

title: Spacetime Emergence in the Memory of a Learning Agent
abstract: We show that the causal structure of spacetime can emerge within the memory of a learning agent performing a quantum information task. We train a model-based reinforcement-learning agent to maximize the quantum mutual information between localized quantum probes interacting with a quantum field in Minkowski spacetime, without directly providing it with information regarding the spacetime metric or causal structure. In learning to accomplish this task, the reinforcement-learning agent constructs an internal predictive model whose planner develops the characteristic null structure of spacetime, allowing us to reconstruct the causal structure of the Minkowski metric with high accuracy. Within this task, spacetime geometry is obtained from an agent's successful predictions and actions, providing a first step toward showing that spacetime concepts emerge from operational quantum experience.

title: MemShift: Separating Detection from Repair in LLM-Derived Personal Memory
abstract: AI assistants store values that a language model derived from a person's records under the person's own definitions, such as their important contacts. Keeping such a value correct takes two steps: detection, noticing that an input changed, and repair, producing the correct new value. Benchmarks that score only the final answer cannot tell which step failed, and they state every change as new text. Seeing this limitation, we present MemShift, a benchmark of five shifts: source revision, deletion, redefinition, writer switch, and export. The first three fork a synthetic world into branches that differ only in the shift. Gold values and dependencies are fixed before any text, and a deterministic scorer replaces an LLM judge. For a memory that reports its invalidations, MemShift shows for each changed item whether the memory noticed the change and whether its repair was right. Moreover, we build a reference memory with known detection and repair to validate the measure. By evaluating four open-weight LLMs, we find that detection helps only as much as repair allows: the LLMs re-derive few values computed by the person's definitions correctly, and programs that the LLM writes over typed records close most of the gap to exact recomputation. Code and data are available at https://github.com/zichuanxu/memshift.

title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
abstract: Abstract A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff—that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. I(W;R) measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy. evidence.title: When Does Less Information Pay? An Exact Finite Atlas of Representation, Payoff, and Cost
evidence.abstract: Abstract A representation that retains one bit about a four-state world can solve a task perfectly, while another that retains 1.5 bits on average reaches only 75% accuracy. The difference lies in which distinctions each representation preserves. We examine this relationship in a uniform four-state world by enumerating all admissible representations and binary action rules. Constructions are compared both by replacing one component while holding the others fixed and by choosing the best action rule separately for each module. We consider three tasks, their mixtures, and four separate hypothetical cost tariffs. In some comparisons, the representation retaining less world information has the higher payoff; in others, the more informative representation does. There are also pairs with different information amounts but equal payoff—that is, equal task accuracy. If a representation preserves all existing distinctions and adds new ones, its best zero-cost payoff cannot decrease. Lower-information advantages therefore depend on which distinctions are retained. Equal counts of opposing advantages under representation replacement follow from coding symmetry. In broader comparisons, the shares depend on how repeated realizations are counted. A different task set or resource price can change which member of a fixed pair performs better. These results are exact, complete censuses of the specified finite sets of constructions and comparisons. The atlas provides a reproducible worked model for examining how action constraints, counting rules, and cost assumptions affect comparisons. It illustrates established distinctions between information quantity and decision value rather than proposing a new general law of their relation. I(W;R) measures retained world information, and payoff measures task accuracy. title: DynaSolver: A Neural Operator for Autoregressive 4D Flow Prediction with Dynamic Boundaries
abstract: Neural operators provide efficient surrogates for computational fluid dynamics (CFD), but most are designed for static geometries and are not equipped to model unsteady flows induced by continuously moving boundaries. We study dynamic-boundary 4D CFD prediction for articulated moving geometries and introduce RoboCFD-4D, a temporally resolved robotic CFD benchmark spanning diverse morphologies and flow conditions. To address the computational and autoregressive challenges of this setting, we propose DynaSolver, a neural operator that explicitly conditions on boundary evolution and causal flow history. DynaSolver employs an efficient physical-token formulation that amortizes point-to-token projection across the operator stack, substantially reducing repeated point-space spatio-temporal computation while retaining accurate point-level reconstruction. We further introduce Replay-Augmented Parallel Training, which exposes the model to autoregressively generated histories while preserving parallel dense supervision, narrowing the gap between ground-truth-conditioned training and autoregressive rollout. Experiments on RoboCFD-4D show that DynaSolver achieves the best full-rollout accuracy among a broad range of learned CFD surrogates, with its advantage increasing as rollout proceeds, indicating substantially reduced autoregressive error accumulation. Project page: https://made-gpt.github.io/DynaSolver-ProjectPage.

title: LEANGUARD: Lean-Verified Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
abstract: Tool-using language-model agents often execute actions that their domain policies forbid. We present LeanGuard, a runtime that checks every proposed tool call against a policy written in Lean4 before the call reaches the environment. Policies combine state predicates with scoped past-time temporal operators over the execution history, evaluation is fail-closed, and the decision procedure is proved equivalent to a LeanLTL semantics. A denied call can be corrected in two ways. With feedback, the agent receives the violated rule and a hint; with proof-guided repair, Lean metaprogramming searches for a nearby call that preserves the user's intent and proves that the policy admits it, without the model. On Tau-Bench with five Qwen models (0.8B-27B), unguarded agents execute at least 33 calls that the Lean policy forbids, while LeanGuard executes none; with feedback, task success does not change significantly. On DTap, LeanGuard reduces direct prompt-injection success from 57.9% to 5.9%, and in telecom, where benign tasks need no writes, benign success is unchanged. Feedback reduces repeated blocked calls and raises task success for four of five models over a bare denial. On replayed denials, repair proves an admissible edit for 88 of 252 denials caused by argument values, in a median of 2,ms.

title: From Multi-Agent Models to Enterprise Intelligent Agents: An AI-Powered Knowledge Compilation and Production Optimisation Platform for Oil and Gas Field Development
abstract: Abstract Oil and gas field development planning remains a slow, expert-dependent workflow, with multi-year plans scattered across subsidiaries in heterogeneous formats and tacit knowledge locked in individual experts. This paper presents an enterprise scientific research agent that compiles development plans into a unified knowledge base and enables autonomous scheme generation, simulation and continuous optimisation at enterprise scale. The architecture fuses a 240-indicator standardised ontology, multi-modal LLM knowledge compilation, a lifecycle-aware knowledge graph (facts, states, events), a RAG-augmented three-tier memory, long-horizon multi-agent orchestration (Build and Optimize modes with frozen-evidence acceptance), a unified MCP tool bus, and a git-style model relation tree that makes every run traceable and reversible. The platform has compiled 2,924 development plans across 14 subsidiaries of a national oil company. In a black-oil case, the agent autonomously generated water-flooding well-pattern schemes in two hours without human intervention, raising the ten-year recovery factor from 18.9% to 34.6% against a 30% target, while planning-cycle latency was substantially reduced. The results confirm that progressing from multi-agent research models to unified enterprise intelligent agents is a scalable path toward knowledge-driven decision-making in large, multi-asset petroleum portfolios.

title: Evaluating Uncertainty Calibration in Probabilistic Time Series Foundation Models
abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) are increasingly used for probabilistic forecasting across diverse domains, yet the reliability of their uncertainty estimates remains poorly understood. In this work, we study uncertainty calibration in probabilistic TSFMs from a broader methodological and empirical perspective. We introduce a taxonomy of how TSFMs represent predictive uncertainty and develop a fine-grained evaluation framework for calibration in multi-horizon forecasting that distinguishes pooled, horizon-wise, and stronger conditional notions of calibration. Using this framework, we conduct a comprehensive empirical evaluation of popular TSFMs across diverse datasets and show that current models exhibit distinct and systematic patterns of miscalibration that standard metrics often obscure. We further analyze common post-hoc recalibration methods and characterize which forms of calibration they can improve and which tend to persist. Our results provide practical guidance for evaluating and improving uncertainty calibration in TSFMs and highlight important limitations of current practice.

title: CSTrainer : An Ontology Driven Multiple AIGC Agentic Approach for Oil and Gas Scientific Research Supporting
abstract: Abstract Scientific research in the energy and oil & gas sector faces significant challenges, including massive heterogeneous data, complex mechanisms, high uncertainty, and substantial reliance on expert experience. While recent advancements in generative AI offer autonomy in multi-step reasoning, generic models offered limitations such as hallucinations, insufficient domain knowledge, and poor alignment with researchers' prior works. To address the need for continuity in research trajectories, this study proposes CSTrainer, an ontology-driven, multi-agent system designed for energy-specific scientific research assistance. CSTrainer integrates 5 foundational models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek, Qwen, Tencent-Hunyuan, and Doubao-Seed (five foundation LLMs)) and employs a hierarchical architecture featuring multi-agent clusters, cross-model voting, and debate mechanisms. A core innovation is its use of a distributed dynamic ontology framework, which constrains reasoning paths to ensure scientific rigour and mitigate hallucinations. The system facilitates end-to-end research support, encompassing scientific problem formulation, technical route planning, ontology construction, and executable workflow generation, augmented by weighted Bayesian updating and lightweight human-in-the-loop (HIL) feedback. The system was validated on 3 datasets: UNISIM-IV (open), tight gas well re-evaluation (proprietary), and transnational pipeline scheduling (proprietary). Results demonstrate that CSTrainer achieves stable, high quality performance for 3–5 scientific questions extraction, outperforming agent-only baselines by 62.5%–87.5%. While 10 rounds of detailed human feedback yielded optimal results, excessive interaction or scaling beyond 10 problems induced instability. The system attained full marks in the tight gas re-evaluation scenario, confirming its efficacy in bridging the gap between conceptual research and engineering implementation. CSTrainer provides a scalable, interpretable, and controllable AI-for-science pathway for industrial research. Keywords: Ontology; Scientific research supporting; Energy engineering research; Multi-Agent; Generative AI

title: A Scaling Theory of Multi-Epoch Pretraining: Late-Time Overfitting and Ensembling
abstract: In the near future language model pretraining will become bound by total data rather than total compute. Such a regime requires revisiting scaling laws and scaling law theory. Motivated by prior works that have found utility in ensembling, we study how the number of training epochs and ensemble size jointly shape generalization when training data are fixed. In language-model experiments on FineWeb, logit averaging reduces late-training deterioration, delays optimal stopping, and can outperform wider or deeper single models at matched parameter-token budgets over a common training horizon. To analyze this interaction between data reuse and ensembling, we derive a dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) for multi-epoch stochastic gradient descent in power-law random-feature ensembles, tracking error correlations across epochs and models. Ensembling reduces the prediction variance responsible for late-time growth in expected test error, changing the optimal stopping time. We use these stopping times to derive compute-allocation laws at fixed data and individual model sizes. Under this allocation, ensemble size grows with compute at least as fast as training time per member, while excess test loss above the limiting loss decreases as a power of compute.

title: 3D-BBDA: Backpropagation-Free Black-Box Domain Adaptation for Robust 3D Point Cloud Recognition
abstract: Robust 3D point-cloud recognition is critical for robotics, mapping, and urban sensing, yet point-cloud classifiers often suffer performance drops under domain shifts caused by sensor changes, environmental variation, and acquisition artifacts. Many existing adaptation methods are difficult to deploy in practice because they require access to source data or the internal parameters of the source model, which may be restricted by privacy, licensing, or security constraints. We present 3D-BBDA, a backpropagation-free black-box domain adaptation framework that adapts a source-trained predictor to unlabeled target data using only black-box outputs. Our method performs pseudo-label guided prototype-based alignment and employs a weighted prediction module to fuse source logits with alignment logits, reducing sensitivity to noisy pseudo-labels. To stabilize prototype memory when pseudo-label coverage is incomplete, we construct a Gaussian-perturbed prototype prior from unlabeled target predictions and use it as a fallback for missing or unreliable class prototypes during alignment. Experiments on four corrupted 3D benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines. On ModelNet-40C, 3D-BBDA achieves mean errors of 32.08% (PointNet) and 29.62% (GDANet), outperforming Source-only (35.88% / 34.03%) and BFTT3D (33.78% / 32.36%). 3D-BBDA requires only a single forward pass with no gradient updates making it suitable for real-time, privacy-preserving deployment in transferable 3D recognition pipelines. Project page is available at https://visdomlab.github.io/3D_BBDA

title: When Similarity is Not Enough: Deterministic Retrieval Pathways for Wellbore-Accurate Knowledge Synthesis on the Volve Field
abstract: This study compares similarity-based retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) with deterministic retrieval pathways for question answering over the 1,266 public daily drilling reports of Equinor's Volve field. The objective is to establish where embedding similarity is an adequate retrieval mechanism for an identifier-dense operational archive, and where it has to be replaced by the explicit structure the reports already carry, so that an answer about a named wellbore cannot come from a neighboring sidetrack. Reports rendered from the Wellsite Information Transfer Standard Markup Language (WITSML) were parsed into typed sections and organized as a hierarchical corpus tree spanning field, wellbore, report, and section, yielding 7,564 retrievable section chunks. A rule-based router classifies each query and lifts exact filters for wellbore, date, year, section, operator, and rig. Structured intents are answered by walking the tree deterministically, while conceptual intents retain dense and lexical retrieval under weighted rank fusion, and a metadata gate restricts every well-named query to the named wellbore before any ranking. Performance was assessed on 114 queries generated from the corpus across six classes, using recall@10, mean reciprocal rank (MRR), nDCG@10, set precision, recall, F1, date ordering, and a wrong-well rate. Similarity-only configurations proved inadequate for the structured questions that dominate this corpus. The best similarity baseline reached recall@10 = 0.16 on section navigation and F1 = 0.44 on report aggregation, and no similarity configuration returned a chronology in date order, while the deterministic pathways scored 1.00 on all three. On identifier lookups the gated system retrieved the named report at recall 1.00, against 0.18 for the strongest ungated ranker, with a wrong-well rate of zero, and routing lifted within-well operational correlation from F1 = 0.33 to F1 = 0.75. Ungated lexical ranking drew results from the wrong wellbore on 84% of identifier queries and on 52% of structural queries, which confirms that wrong-well retrieval is not confined to neural encoders. A controlled tokenizer comparison placed sibling wellbore identifiers at a mean cosine of 0.32 under subword character n-grams against 0.15 for unrelated identifiers, while identifier-preserving word tokens held both at 0.00, and gating returned the subword encoder to a wrong-well rate of zero. Conceptual paraphrase marks the boundary of the deterministic claim, where the tree alone scored 0.00 and the routed system retained recall@10 = 0.17.

title: FedReady: Bounded Agents for Federation Formation
abstract: Federated learning (FL) runtimes standardize aggregation and deployment, but each new study still requires federation formation: selecting task-eligible sites and preparing their local data and task code for federated training or analysis. This preparation recurs when the target changes, while raw records and site-private mappings are excluded from cross-site FL messages. We present FedReady, a system that performs federation formation with bounded LLM agents. Agents propose shared contracts, local adapters, and task code; the runtime owns workflow state and accepts artifacts only after checks tied to their digests. Candidate site discovery prioritizes recall; local eligibility verification checks task support before site admission. Once participating sites and artifacts are fixed, conventional federated training or analysis proceeds without readiness agents. Across 39 simulated retinal sites and four tasks, discovery reaches recall 1.00 at precision 0.65; local eligibility verification removes all 17 false positives without losing an eligible site-task pair. The participating sites supply 45,575 task-record instances and complete four 100-round jobs, including one with a runtime-generated contract. Across ten patient cohorts, preparation supports seven patient populations and holds endpoints at three sources as unsupported. Comparison with manually prepared reference populations and analysis (the manual reference) gives a maximum survival-curve difference of 0.001133. We also analyze 19 development failures, targeted classification ablations, and standalone and heterogeneous agent configurations. These results establish the feasibility of task-specific data preparation before ordinary FL training or analysis.

title: From Pilot to Enterprise Scale: Lessons Learned from Delivering Ai Solutions Across Diverse Industries and Stakeholder Ecosystems
abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has rapidly evolved from experimental proof-of-concepts to a strategic enabler of business transformation across industries. Despite significant investments in AI technologies, many organizations continue to struggle with moving successful pilots into scalable enterprise-wide deployments. While technical feasibility is often demonstrated during pilot phases, challenges related to stakeholder alignment, governance, change management, user adoption, data readiness, and operational integration frequently limit the realization of sustainable business value. As AI solutions become increasingly embedded within critical business processes, organizations require structured approaches to bridge the gap between innovation and large-scale implementation. This paper presents practical lessons learned from coordinating and delivering AI solutions across diverse industries, organizational structures, and stakeholder ecosystems. The objective is to identify key success factors that enable organizations to transition from isolated AI pilots to enterprise-scale deployments while maximizing adoption, business impact, and long-term sustainability. The study examines a portfolio of AI initiatives involving multiple stakeholders, including business leaders, domain experts, technical teams, governance functions, and end users operating across different sectors and geographic regions. The approach focuses on the end-to-end AI delivery lifecycle, from opportunity identification and pilot development to enterprise deployment and operationalization. A structured delivery framework was established incorporating stakeholder engagement, governance alignment, business value definition, agile execution, user enablement, and adoption monitoring. Special attention was given to managing diverse stakeholder expectations, facilitating collaboration between technical and non-technical teams, and ensuring alignment between AI capabilities and business objectives. The framework also emphasizes iterative value realization through continuous feedback loops, performance measurement, and scalable operating models that support expansion across business units and functions. Lessons learned from deployment challenges, adoption barriers, and organizational readiness assessments were systematically analyzed to identify recurring patterns and critical success factors. The findings demonstrate that successful AI scaling is driven less by technological sophistication and more by organizational readiness, stakeholder engagement, and governance maturity. Projects that established clear business outcomes, executive sponsorship, and cross-functional collaboration achieved significantly higher adoption rates and sustained business value compared with technology-centric implementations. title: Sonar-MoE: In-Backward Expert Updates for Memory-Efficient Mixture-of-Experts Training
abstract: Most parameters of a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model belong to its experts, and standard training keeps every expert gradient in GPU memory until the optimizer step. This memory grows with the number and size of the experts, so it rises as MoE models scale. We introduce Sonar-MoE, which updates each expert tensor during the backward pass and frees its gradient right away. It brings optimizer-in-backward from dense models to batched MoE expert tensors, so the GPU never holds more than one layer of expert gradients. When we fine-tune OLMoE-1B-7B and Granite-3.1-3B-A800M in bf16 with two expert-kernel backends, Sonar-MoE lowers peak memory by 19% to 22%. Its updates are bitwise identical to standard training without expert gradient clipping, and held-out loss stays within 0.003 of all baselines. Each step also takes 17% to 23% less time than standard training with global-norm clipping. Updating whole batched tensors rather than individual experts is what keeps Sonar-MoE fast, as it avoids a 20% to 72% slowdown while using the same memory. Sonar-MoE matches optimizer-in-backward over all parameters in memory and speed while still clipping the dense parameters.

title: A Stable Attribution Is Not a Stable Error Rate: What Feature-Attribution Monitoring Can See Under Drift, Why 'More Sensitive Than the Inputs' and 'Silent While Fairness Fails' Are Both Correct, and the Label-Free Statistic the Fairness Alarm Needed
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Deployed classifiers are often monitored without labels, and feature attributions are one of the signals watched: a production monitoring service alerts when the ranking of SHAP attributions moves, and one line of work argues that the explanation space is more sensitive than the input space to shifts that matter. A 2026 study reports the other face: on COMPAS under injected feature noise, TreeSHAP explanations stayed largely stable while the protected group's false positive rate rose from 37.84 to 70.39 percent. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the two findings concern different objects. Per-instance attributions, the distribution of attribution vectors, a top-k ranking of mean absolute attributions and an attribution of the loss are four instruments; only the last uses labels, and only the second sees everything the prediction distribution sees. The paper orders the label-free observables into a ladder, derives which group fairness quantities each rung can read, and shows that a group false positive rate is readable from none of them without an assumption about how outcomes given features changed. The anchor study's own numbers add two results: its disparity widened as a difference and narrowed as a ratio, and, with labels fixed, its false-positive rises imply rises in each group's positive-prediction rate, which needs no labels to compute, unless a group has almost no true negatives. The paper gives a decision procedure for choosing and reading a label-free fairness monitor and names the studies that would settle what remains open.

title: Integrating Structural Geology and Remote Sensing for Hydrothermal Alteration Mapping and Gold Exploration Targeting at the WG03 Prospect, Keraf Zone, Northern Sudan
abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope This study aims to integrate structural geology and remote sensing techniques to investigate hydrothermal alteration patterns and structural controls on gold mineralization within the WG03 Prospect (Al Nuqara Area) of the Keraf Shear Zone, Northern Sudan. The work evaluates the role of shear zone architecture, deformation patterns, and hydrothermal systems in improving mineral exploration targeting within the Arabian-Nubian Shield. Methods, Procedures, Process The study combines structural field mapping, geological interpretation, petrographic observations, and remote sensing analysis using ASTER and Landsat imagery. Hydrothermal alteration zones were identified through spectral band ratios and image enhancement techniques integrated within a GIS-based framework. Structural lineament extraction, deformation analysis, and lithological interpretation were combined with field observations and geochemical data to evaluate the spatial relationship between structural corridors, alteration systems, and gold mineralization within the study area. Results, Observations, and Conclusions The integrated analysis revealed that gold mineralization within the WG03 Prospect is strongly controlled by reactivated shear structures and localized brittle-ductile deformation zones associated with the Keraf Shear Zone system. Remote sensing analysis delineated relative spectral responses that were compared with field-identified alteration and mineralized structural corridors. Alteration signatures identified include silicification, sericitization, chloritization, and iron oxide enrichment associated with structurally focused fluid pathways. Structural interpretation indicates that deformation reactivation, lithological competency contrasts, and fracture permeability collectively influenced hydrothermal fluid migration and ore deposition. The integration of structural geology and remote sensing provided a basis for prioritizing exploration targets and demonstrated the importance of multidisciplinary geoscience workflows for mineral exploration in underexplored Precambrian terranes. Novel/Additive Information This study presents an integrated exploration workflow combining structural geology, GIS, and satellite remote sensing for hydrothermal alteration mapping and gold exploration targeting within the Keraf Shear Zone of the Arabian-Nubian Shield. The work contributes new insights into structurally controlled mineralization within Sudanese gold-bearing terranes and demonstrates the practical application of integrated geoscience approaches for mineral exploration and resource targeting.

title: BISECT: Bilevel Spectral Decomposition for Low-Rank Continual Learning
abstract: Exemplar-free continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers increasingly relies on Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), yet prevailing methods govern the low-rank update space through strict subspace isolation. By projecting each incoming task into the approximate null space of historical token activations, isolation-based learners equate any cross-task feature overlap with catastrophic interference. We show that this orthogonality premise induces a structural bottleneck we term \emph{spectral starvation}: when down-projection bases are locked before task optimization, the gradient norm reaching the trainable up-projection is upper-bounded by the energy of current-task features captured by the chosen basis. Because natural visual tasks share low- and mid-level covariance structure, historical null tails contain barely $5.5\%$ of incoming task variance, starving new-class plasticity while blocking positive consolidation along shared directions. We propose BISECT (Bilevel Spectral Decomposition), a continual LoRA framework that partitions a fixed rank-$r$ budget into two orthogonal functional blocks: an invariant carrier spanned by the dominant modes of the joint historical-and-current Gram matrix, and a novelty complement extracted via generalized Rayleigh whitening followed by orthogonal complement projection. After single-task training, BISECT folds both blocks back into the frozen backbone using a closed-form precision gate that scales each rank-1 invariant atom by its current-to-joint Rayleigh ratio while preserving novelty atoms at unit gain. Across eight incremental settings on ImageNet-R, ImageNet-A, CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and DomainNet, BISECT outperforms prompt, adapter, and LoRA baselines with zero extra inference parameters or FLOPs, and remains complementary to sparse analytic expansion.

title: PlantVLM-Edge: Quantized Vision-Language Models for On-Device Crop Health Diagnosis
abstract: Timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is essential for sustainable agricultural production, yet accurate diagnosis often requires expert knowledge that is not readily available. Recent vision-language models (VLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in visual understanding, reasoning, and natural-language interaction, creating new opportunities for intelligent crop health assessment. However, deploying VLMs on resource-constrained devices remains challenging due to their substantial computational and memory requirements. This paper presents PlantVLM-Edge, a quantized vision-language framework for conversational crop health diagnosis that can run entirely on resource-constrained edge devices. PlantVLM-Edge combines agricultural domain adaptation, post-training quantization, and on-device serving with an offline chat interface, allowing growers to ask open-ended questions and receive diagnoses, symptom explanations, and management guidance without cloud connectivity. The framework is backbone-agnostic: we validate it with two different VLM types with varying scale and architecture (Qwen3-VL-2B and LLaVA-1.5-7B), four quantization schemes, and two diagnostic domains (plant diseases and insect pests), and we deploy all variants on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Eight-bit quantization affects answer quality minimally relative to the full-precision model, and 4-bit activation-aware weight quantization (AWQ) retains 98.6% of full-precision answer quality on both domains while reducing the weight memory of the 2B backbone by 49%. In its most compact form, PlantVLM-Edge requires 2.01 GiB of weight memory, returns its first token in about 0.12 s, and completes a 64-token diagnostic response in 0.78 s. These results demonstrate that timely and accurate crop health diagnosis is practical on edge devices, providing a foundation for next-generation crop monitoring and decision support systems.

title: MCP Tool Poisoning in Agentic AI Frameworks: A Cross-Framework Measurement Study
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets agentic AI frameworks connect language models to external tool providers, but it carries attacker-controlled content (tool descriptions, schema fields, and response data) into model context without validation. Prior benchmarks measure model compliance with poisoned instructions without confirming real execution. We present the first cross-framework measurement of MCP tool poisoning with real tool execution. A 25-class root-cause taxonomy unifies prior classifications, and the open-source tool mcpvenom drives a 9,720-cell susceptibility matrix across 12 frameworks, 18 models, and 45 attack scenarios, with a dual oracle that confirms exfiltration via canary HTTP receipt. The overall attack success rate is 22.9% (2,113 vulnerable cells). Of these, 64.9% dispatch an attacker tool call, 23.0% contact the attacker endpoint, and 12.1% verifiably exfiltrate a secret. Resistance is model-level: nine core frameworks cluster within 23 to 26% (chi-squared = 3.30, p = 0.91), and no framework implements intentional defense. Incidental framework properties mitigate in specific cases, and a regex description scanner rejects 20 of 45 scenarios at a 7.2% false-positive rate, so metadata scanning alone is a partial control. Model ASR ranges from 0.4% to 49.7%. Claude Opus 4.8 is vulnerable in 8 of 530 cells while issuing 223 explicit refusals. A code-level audit finds no intentional defense across twelve frameworks, and all five coordinated disclosures across four vendors were rejected.

title: Nonparametric Intensity Estimation for Covariate-Driven Poisson Processes Using Deep Learning
abstract: We consider nonparametric maximum likelihood estimation of the intensity function of a Poisson process, allowing the intensity to depend on observed covariates. Such models describe how event rates vary with external conditions, including conditions under which the intensity becomes arbitrarily small or vanishes. However, risk analysis based on the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence typically requires the true intensity to be bounded away from zero, a restrictive assumption in applications. We develop a unified approach that avoids this assumption and derive an oracle inequality for the covariate-averaged Hellinger distance between the true intensity and the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE). As an application of the oracle inequality, we establish convergence rates for NPMLEs based on deep neural networks (DNNs). Our results show that, as in nonparametric regression, the ability of DNNs to capture underlying structure leads to improved convergence rates. Specifically, DNN-based NPMLEs mitigate the curse of dimensionality when the true intensity has a compositional structure and automatically adapt to a low-dimensional Riemannian manifold structure of the event space. For intensity functions with a compositional structure, DNN-based NPMLEs achieve nearly minimax-optimal convergence rates without explicitly incorporating this structure into the network architecture. Simulations demonstrate that DNN-based estimators outperform kernel estimators in most settings, while manifold kernels remain competitive in some designs. Finally, we analyze stimulus-evoked neural spiking using data from the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels project. DNN-based NPMLEs provide better out-of-sample performance than a conditional kernel estimator, as evaluated by held-out log-likelihood.

title: Can LLM Agents Be Forward-Deployed Engineers? Requirement Discovery and Delivery for Enterprise Text-to-SQL
abstract: LLM coding agents can increasingly automate model post-training, but whether they can act as forward-deployed engineer (FDE) agents, discovering customer requirements and turning them into deployment decisions, remains unclear. We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.

title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.

title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
abstract: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.

evidence.title: Variational Functional Neural Networks (vfNN)
evidence.abstract: We present a variational functional neural network (vfNN) algorithm that optimizes physically motivated continuum functionals in integral form (e.g., Lagrangian, Hamiltonian, or free energy) to find the states of a system. That way, vfNN bypasses solving the equations of motion (a.k.a. the Euler-Lagrange equations), which are in the form of differential equations. To this end, our approach is fundamentally different from conventional physics-informed neural networks (PINN) that solve differential equations by minimizing a phenomenological loss function involving higher order derivatives and ad hoc weight factors. In contrast, vfNN merely evaluates lower order derivatives of the generating functional and replaces the weight factors with rigorous physical scales. This also fundamentally changes the loss landscape, and the desired solutions may become unstable. For this emergent nonconvex optimization problem, we develop a quasi-Newton optimization algorithm with simulated annealing that converges to the solutions of the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations of the functional regardless of their stability properties. Our simulations using vfNN give accurate results for benchmark systems governed by linear or nonlinear ordinary differential equations.

title: An Agentic Framework for Automated Power System Studies and Grid Connection Assessment
abstract: Connecting new generation and demand to the grid depends on two scarce skills: checking applications against a large, changing body of regulation, and running the network studies that decide where and how a project connects. We present Grid Agents, an AI system that brings both together, and the methodology we use to evaluate it. The Grid Ontology is its knowledge system. It represents the regulation, standards and engineering knowledge that grid work depends on, makes it searchable, and evolves as the agents learn from use. Every answer drawn from it rests on evidence the agents cite. Grid Studio is an agent system specialised for power-system engineering. It works in its own engineering environment with domain tools and a study framework, draws on the Grid Ontology, and relies on established solvers for every number it reports. In both, engineers make the decisions. We bring eight published power-system benchmark families, previously scattered across separate papers, into one suite of 519 tasks, and we verify not only each answer but the work behind it, by replaying the agent's tool calls. The Grid Ontology cites the right regulatory evidence more often than a general coding agent or retrieval pipelines, leads on LegalBench-RAG and ranks first on the public leaderboards of the Enterprise RAG Challenge and ViDoRe V3. Grid Studio scores highest on the 519 power-system tasks and is the fastest of all the systems we compare, both by a statistically significant margin. With an optimiser in the loop, its reinforcement packages cost 33-67% less on average than those the agent designs alone.

title: ParaDeAl: Parallel Descent Algorithms for Sparse Statistics
abstract: Best subset selection is a central problem in statistical regression, drawing increasing attention from the broader optimization and machine learning communities. Solving the hard L0 sparsity constraint directly has been computationally challenging; as a result, most existing work proposes formulations which do not enforce the constraint, but instead use a mix of L0/L1/L2 penalties to encourage sparsity. Modern methods for solving such penalized formulations are tractable for p = 100,000, but give up direct control over sparsity. In this paper, we propose a two-stage proximal gradient descent-based approach which both enforces the sparsity constraint and incorporates L1/L2 penalties, leveraging GPUs for computational acceleration to find approximate solutions. Our method, ParaDeAl, offers the user the ability to select the problem hyperparameters, solves all configurations in parallel, and obtains solutions up to 15x faster than the best state-of-the-art CPU competitors while achieving almost identical test accuracy for the same support size for large (p > 100,000) synthetic and real-world datasets.

title: Grading the Unannotated: Insights from the WorkRB Skill Extraction Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026
abstract: Skill extraction benchmarks score models against a few human-annotated positives and treat every other skill in the vocabulary as equally wrong. At the scale of ESCO (13,939 skills) this binary view can reward models that rank the annotated positive high for the wrong reason, and hides semantically nonsensical predictions. The WorkRB Challenge at RecSys-HR 2026 replaces it with graded relevance: every candidate skill in a model's ranking window carries a 0 to 4 grade, and the leaderboard scores nDCG@100 against these grades. Since ternary judgements proved too coarse for objective annotation, relevance is decomposed into a cascade of four binary questions (same domain, activity mentioned, right granularity, replacement of a gold positive) that a smaller LLM judge can answer reliably; the labels are validated with blind human and frontier-model re-annotation. This paper documents the annotation methodology, the construction of five benchmark datasets (four with vacancy sentences as queries, one with lexically distant skill surface forms), the validation of the LLM cascade, and insights from the submissions. The field converged on multi-stage retrieve-and-rerank pipelines, whose gains come from clearing nonsense out of the ranking window rather than finding more positives: at the top of the leaderboard, the graded ordering is uncorrelated with what binary evaluation would have said. Graded labels expose much bigger gaps between top submissions and baselines than binary evaluation does, and show that semantic-understanding skill recommendation is still wide open. The clear next direction is bringing efficiency back: every submitted system we could size uses at least 42x, typically several hundred times, more parameters than the baselines it beats.

title: DistDebug-Bench: Can LLM Agents Diagnose Bugs in Distributed Systems?
abstract: LLM agents show strong potential in software engineering tasks such as competitive programming and code synthesis. Existing benchmarks, however, largely focus on small-scale settings such as self-contained Python modules, leaving distributed systems, an essential class of production software, under-examined. We introduce DistDebug-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating agents' ability to diagnose complex-system failures at the code level. It curates 120 high-quality real-world bugs from 11 widely used distributed systems, spanning 5 programming languages and 10 failure patterns. Through an extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art LLMs and agents, we identify substantial gaps between current agents and real-world debugging tasks. A recurring gap is tunnel vision due to a lack of explicit reasoning structure and nondeterminism from inconsistent tool-use scope. The benchmark and evaluator are available at https://github.com/OrderLab/distdebug-bench, with agent traces and a leaderboard at https://distdebug.com.

title: PanoTac: A Dense Three-Axis Tactile Sensor for Robust Touch-Centric Manipulation
abstract: Contact-rich manipulation benefits from tactile feedback that captures both detailed contact geometry and interaction forces. When scooping grains, contact patterns help infer spoon orientation, while resistance transmitted through the grasp guides motion. To provide these complementary sensing capabilities, we present PanoTac, a low-cost, compliant tactile fingertip designed for dense three-axis tactile sensing. Each fingertip provides a $12 \times 32 \times 3$ tactile representation, with one normal ($z$) and two shear ($x$, $y$) response components at each taxel. The sensor operates at 60 Hz and costs less than $50 per fingertip. Sensor characterization quantifies response repeatability and consistency across sensor instances and contact locations. We integrate PanoTac into a robotic system with a visuo-tactile pipeline. Across test-tube preparation, grain scooping, and salt pouring, the resulting policies outperform vision-only baselines by an average of 46.7 percentage points. Ablations show that removing either spatial contact information or shear feedback reduces overall performance across the task suite. Our project page is available at https://panotac.github.io.

title: VIAS: Value-Isolating Activation Steering for Multi-Value Alignment and Compliance for Organisations
abstract: Organisations increasingly deploy large language model agents that must follow organisational values. We check whether activation steering, which adds vectors to a model's internal activations during generation without changing its weights, can improve compliance beyond prompting alone. Since most scenarios involve several values at once, we focus on multi-value steering. A simple way to build these vectors is to contrast responses that follow all values relevant to a scenario with responses that violate them. However, this gives nearly identical vectors for different values: they capture a general compliance signal rather than individual values, which limits their use when combining several values. We propose Value-Isolating Activation Steering (VIAS), which contrasts responses to the same scenario under two prompts, one listing all relevant values and one omitting a single target value. We keep a pair only if the target value changes from compliant to non-compliant and both responses still meet a minimum compliance level on the other values. We evaluate VIAS on PROTECT, a workplace compliance dataset where each scenario is tagged with relevant values from a 21-value taxonomy. VIAS reduces overlap between value vectors, making them better suited for multi-value steering, although this alone does not lead to independent control over each value. Combined with prompting, VIAS complies with every tagged value on 69.6% of scenarios for Qwen2.5-7B, 75.2% for Mistral-7B, and 72.6% for Phi-3.5-mini, outperforming prompting alone for all three models.

title: RASP: Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity Continual Learning in a Stationary-Size LoRA
abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning on pre-trained Vision Transformers largely relies on a costly premise: preventing catastrophic forgetting requires either spawning a dedicated LoRA branch per session---causing adapter parameters to scale linearly with task horizon---or applying sparse Mixture-of-Experts gating symmetrically to both forward and backward passes, which sacrifices representational rank at test time. We argue that reading consolidated knowledge and writing new task credit are fundamentally asymmetric operations. Because visual features in a shared low-rank space distribute across rank-1 atoms rather than localizing in disjoint task silos, forward inference should read all atoms at full rank capacity, whereas backward optimization should restrict plasticity to a sparse subset of input-aligned channels. We introduce RASP (Read-All, Sparse-Plasticity LoRA), which adapts a single stationary-size adapter across sequential tasks. At each step, a scene-modulated cosine router selects the top-$q$ unlocked atoms to receive gradients, blocks updates on the remaining $r-q$ channels, and penalizes Frobenius Gram coherence between active and non-updated output directions. Across sessions, the router's empirical activation trace and each atom's exact spectral norm form a zero-overhead geometric consolidation index $ω_j = \sqrt{\tilde{c}_j \tildeσ_j}$ that drives Cauchy step attenuation and boundary anchor locking. Across CIFAR-100, CUB-200, ImageNet-R, and ImageNet-A, RASP matches or surpasses branch-expanding LoRA learners under a strictly constant parameter footprint.

title: ST-GFM: Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting with Measured Perturbation Bounds and Masked Spectral Reconstruction
abstract: Graph forecasters for sensor networks are trained in one regime and deployed in others, where sensor coupling and signal frequency content both change. We split this spectral shift into an operator channel and a frequency channel, each with a dimensionless measure. ST-GFM (Spectral-Temporal Graph Forecasting Model) filters every input step with Chebyshev and bidirectional diffusion filters on one learned, non-symmetric operator and alternates them with per-node temporal attention. For the operator channel we prove Frobenius-norm perturbation bounds for both graph branches, show that the Chebyshev bound is attained to first order, and compute its constant from the trained weights and the measured operator norm: 17.9 on METR-LA and 21.5 on PEMS-BAY. Under random edge dropout the trained layer moves by 2.0% to 3.1% of this bound. Masked Spectral Reconstruction (MSR), a self-supervised loss active in the first 40 epochs, matches the log power spectrum of the encoder output to that of the input. For small log-spectral residuals on unclamped bins it is proportional to an Itakura-Saito divergence to leading order. Removing it raises the 60-minute MAE by 0.30 on METR-LA, close to the 0.33 lost when all three self-supervised losses go. Under one shared evaluation pipeline, the 60-minute MAE of ST-GFM is 3.5% below a retrained STAEformer on METR-LA and 13.0% below it on PEMS-BAY. Its 60-minute MAE is 3.0980.017 on METR-LA (five seeds) and 1.5760.006 on PEMS-BAY (three seeds), the lowest PEMS-BAY MAE among twelve published baselines.

title: A Cross-Domain Matrix Engine for Signal Processing and Deep Neural Net Inference
abstract: Matrix multiplication dominates both PHY signal processing and Deep Neural Network (DNN) inference, yet these domains place opposing demands on the matrix engine. Signal processing requires low-latency execution of relatively small matrix operations, whereas DNN inference, particularly at large batch sizes, prioritizes high throughput and energy efficiency for large matrix multiplications. While offering efficient memory access profile, a Systolic Array (SA) adds fill and drain delays per matrix. Those can be amortized for large matrices but not for small matrices. Conversely, a tensor unit completes the kernel in few cycles but would require repeated reads of same operand tiles over large matrices. This makes SA too slow for signal processing and tensor too inefficient for AI. We show that this need not be a choice between systolic and tensor structuring of Multiply-Accumulate (MAC) units. We propose a single engine that operates primarily as a SA and, through low-cost reconfiguration, transforms into a tensor-style engine on a per-operation basis. MUXes create both the spatial reduction adder tree and temporal reduction accumulators from the existing MACs and registers within the systolic array. The proposed reconfigurable SA simulated using modified SCALESim simulator, verified on an Zynq 702 FPGA and synthesized using ASAP 7nm FinFET library. SCALE-Sim simulations shows up to 7.5x lower latency for small complex value PHY kernels. Even on DNN workloads, it achieves up to 1.65x speedups over vanilla SA execution with trivial increase of memory accesses, retaining the systolic array's memory access advantage. Synthesis results estimate reconfigurable fabric costs only 8% power and 13.6% area overheads.
